body.hook: You belong to dozens of groups: your family, your friend group, your class, your team, maybe a group chat with 200 people you've never met. Some shape who you are; others you'd barely notice leaving. Sociologists explain why.

vocabulary.definition: Two or more people who interact and share a sense of belonging.
A small, close, long-lasting group, such as family or close friends.
A larger, goal-oriented, less personal group, such as a class or workplace.
A social position a person holds.
The behaviour expected of someone with a status.
A group you belong to and feel loyal to.
A group you don't belong to and may feel competitive toward.

study.title: Map My Groups
study.question: How do groups shape who we are?
study.passage:
Part 1, Group map (15 minutes): Draw yourself in the centre. Draw circles for every group you belong to; place the closest ones nearest you. Label each as primary or secondary.
Charles Horton Cooley (1909) called primary groups the "nursery of human nature": we get identity and emotional support from them. Secondary groups exist for a purpose: earning money, learning, playing a sport. A secondary group can become primary (teammates who become close friends).
Part 2, Status and roles (10 minutes): List your statuses (student, sibling, team captain, employee). Ascribed status: given at birth (age, family). Achieved status: earned (captain, honour student). For two statuses, list expected roles. Role conflict: when two roles clash (a big game the same night as a family event).
Part 3, In-groups and out-groups (10 minutes): Discuss school rivalries. How does belonging to an in-group affect how you see out-groups? Robbers Cave study (Sherif, 1954): two groups of boys at camp quickly became hostile through competition and became friendlier after cooperating on shared goals.
Part 4, Group size (10 minutes): Dyads (two people) are intimate but fragile; triads (three) are more stable but can form two-against-one coalitions.
study.source: Original investigation written for this lesson; concepts summarized from introductory sociology sources.

examples.title: Classify
examples.problem: A school math class. Primary or secondary?

examples.title: Status type
examples.problem: Being someone's daughter is what kind of status?

examples.title: Role conflict
examples.problem: A student is captain and also has a part-time shift during a playoff game. What is this?
examples.answer: Role conflict between captain and employee

examples.title: Robbers Cave
examples.problem: What reduced hostility between the groups?
examples.answer: Cooperating on goals that needed both groups (superordinate goals)

practice.q: Who called primary groups the "nursery of human nature"?
How did the Robbers Cave study reduce conflict?
How can in-group loyalty lead to prejudice?
practice.a: Favouring your group can lead to negative views of out-groups.

practice.q: How can a secondary group become primary?
practice.a: Through close, lasting relationships forming over time.

practice.q: Are online groups primary or secondary?
practice.a: They can be either, depending on closeness and purpose.

misconceptions: Thinking all groups affect us equally
Thinking in-group loyalty is always harmless
